title: Tiger or Wind?
sub: Grades 1–2 · The Rustling Bushes · Your brain’s alarm
objective: Children will learn that a part of the brain works like an alarm system, and that it rings loudest when we can’t be sure what is there. Through the Rustling Bushes, they will look for clues to decide *tiger or wind?*, hear why the brain would rather raise a fake alarm than miss a real tiger, and practice three calm steps for when their own alarm rings.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Everyone’s alarm rings sometimes. Knowing why it rings, and how to calm it, helps us be brave.

questions: What did your mind guess first, when you couldn’t see?
What clue told you it was a tiger? What told you it was the wind?
Why would your brain rather ring a fake alarm than miss a tiger?
When has your alarm rung for something that turned out fine?

steps.title: Something in the bushes
script: Ask children to close their eyes. Play the first sound, the rustle, and ask: *“Something is moving in the bushes. What could it be?”* Take guesses: a cat, a bird, a monster, the wind. Play the second sound. *“That one is the wind blowing through the leaves.”* Ask: *“When you couldn’t see, what did your mind guess first?”*

screen.question: Something is moving in the bushes. What could it be?

steps.purpose: Wonder first: a sound, and no way to see what made it.
students: What could be in the bushes?

steps.title: Your brain’s alarm
script: The Fear Lab says a part of your brain called the **amygdala** is your brain’s *alarm system*, and that not being sure sets it off. When the alarm rings, your heart races. Long ago, people who heard a bush rustle and thought *maybe a tiger!* ran away, and stayed safe. The poster says brains are built this way: *it is better to see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator.*

screen.text:
When your brain isn’t sure,
its alarm rings.
screen.cite: Poster 1 · The Science of Being Scared

steps.purpose: Give the feeling a name: an alarm in the brain that rings when we are not sure.
students: Put a hand on your heart.
What does your body do when the alarm rings?

steps.title: Tiger or wind?
script: Show the clue chart. In the Rustling Bushes, a bush rustles in the dark. Sometimes there is a clue: a striped tail tip, a shadow, paw prints or a low growl mean a tiger; leaves blowing loose mean the wind. Sometimes there is no clue at all.

Play two or three rounds together with *Guess first* on, so there is no timer: look, talk it over, then the class calls *“Tiger! Run!”* or *“Just the wind.”* Warn children first that eyes appear suddenly in the dark when it is a tiger; nothing flashes. Turn the sound low or the motion off if you wish.

cells: A striped tail tip, poking out of the bush
A tiger-shaped shadow on the ground
Paw prints leading into the bush
Leaves blowing loose in the wind
Sometimes there isn’t one: talk it over

steps.purpose: Use clues, as a detective does, to tell a real danger from a fake alarm.
students: Look for a clue in the bush.
Talk it over. Then call it: tiger, or just the wind?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Children choose a handout. All three use the same clues from the Rustling Bushes and the same three calm steps.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Draw a line from each clue to *TIGER* or *WIND*, color the three calm steps, draw a bush with a clue, trace *WIND*.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Sort the clues into a tiger column and a wind column, finish a sentence on why the alarm rings, draw a clue for a partner to guess, write what they can do when the alarm rings.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Name each result: fake alarm, missed tiger or tiger spotted. Explain which is worse and why, draw a clue that could trick you, write a tip for a friend whose alarm is ringing.

steps.purpose: Sort clues and practice the calm steps, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same clues and the same calm steps.

steps.title: Three calm steps
script: Practice the three calm steps together: a slow breath in and out, eyes looking round for clues, and naming a grown-up each child could ask. Remind them: *it’s fine for your alarm to ring. It’s trying to keep you safe.*

screen.text:
Stop and breathe.
Look for clues.
Ask a grown-up.

steps.purpose: Leave every child with steps they can use when their own alarm rings.

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* Children show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask a Red Level child the last one.
